newsitem.title: UK: Morgan, Kleinwort set to lead Gazprom ADR - sources.
newsitem.headline: Morgan, Kleinwort set to lead Gazprom ADR - sources.

text.p: Morgan Stanley and Dresdner Bank's Kleinwort Benson are to lead a Global Depositary Receipt and American Depositary Receipt issue for Russia's largest company, RAO Gazprom by the end of the year, banking sources said.
"We have been told to expect the issue before the end of 1996," a financier familiar with the deal said on Wednesday.

However, the deal for the world's biggest natural gas producer has been scaled back from nine percent of the company worth billions of dollars to just one to one and a half percent, around $400 million of stock.
No one at Morgan Stanley or Kleinwort was available to comment on the deal in which Morgan Stanley is expected to be named sole bookrunner.
Gazprom had planned to sell nine percent of the company to overseas investors in 1994, but the deal was delayed due to a slump in Russian share prices.

Now, with the CSFB ROS index of leading Russian shares up from a year low of 525 points to 1,300 points, on the back of Boris Yeltsin's victory in July, the deal is expected to be completed in October or November.
Bankers say that the issue size will be around $400 million and a price equivalent to $1.25 per share is being touted for the overseas offer.
"That means 1.0 to 1.5 percent of the company will be sold," said an oil analyst in London.
However, with Gazprom shares down by one third to 30 cents, in two days trading in Moscow a 95 cent premium looks a little steep, he added.
"People will be prepared to pay quite a high premium for settlement, but that is asking quite a lot," the analyst said.
GDRs and ADRs allow foreign investors to invest in shares without direct currency risk and avoid Russia's chaotic settlement and share trading system.
Despite being Russia's largest company, Gazprom's 23.6 billion shares are among Russia's most illiquid stocks and no paper can change hands without company approval.
Gazprom initially appointed Kleinwort Benson to do the deal in 1994 but the issue became mired in conflicting judgements over how much the company was worth.
Gazprom was reported as believing it could sell a nine percent stake for $25 billion, valuing the company in excess of $278 billion, or three times the market capitalisation of U.S. oil major Exxon.
"It is probably better this way, one percent will whet investor appetites," said the analyst.
The deal which had been expected to be the benchmark in overseas issues by Russian companies was overtaken by others.

In 1995, oil giant LUKoil undertook a $250 million convertible bond issue, which now trades in ADR form and energy company Chernogorneft, utility Mosenergo and the GUM department store all have overseas issues.
Vast political influence is at stake in Gazprom's success.

Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin used to head the company and Pyotr Rodionov, Russia's new minister of fuel and power, was managing director of the company's St Petersburg subsidiary and a board member of Gazprom.

Gazprom's chairman Rem Vyakhirev described Rodionov's appointment earlier this month as "a recognition of Gazprom's collective efforts to ensure reliable supplies of gas for Russia". -- David Chance London newsroom 44 171 542 5887
